description_full: NOV Inc. designs, constructs, manufactures, and sells systems, components, and products for oil and gas drilling and production, and industrial and renewable energy sectors in the United States and internationally. It operates in two segments, Energy Equipment, and Energy Products and Services. The Energy Products and Services segment offers drill bits and borehole enlargement products; independent drilling and intervention downhole tools equipment; frac plugs, frac sleeves, toe initiation burst port systems, and recyclable setting tools; electric submersible pumps, high viscosity pumps, and surface pumps; tubular coating and inspection services for drill-pipe and other oil country tubular goods; solids control and waste management equipment and services; data and digital solutions; precision-engineered drill pipe and drill-stem equipment; connectors and integral thread solutions, including conductor strings, surface casing, and liners; and composite pipe, tanks, and structures. Its Energy Equipment segment provides drilling equipment, such as land rigs, complete offshore drilling packages, and rig components; capital equipment, related consumables, and digital products for hydraulic stimulation, coiled tubing, and wireline services; marine and construction solutions; processing solutions for the separation and treatment of oil, gas, solids, seawater, and produced water production; flexible subsea pipe systems; cavity pumps, specialized mixers and heat exchangers; and reciprocating, multistage, and progressive cavity pumps, midstream products, including closures, transfer pumps, chokes and valves, as well as artificial lift support systems that include production BOPs and stuffing boxes. The company was formerly known as National Oilwell Varco, Inc. and changed its name to NOV Inc. in January 2021. NOV Inc. was founded in 1862 and is based in Houston, Texas.

financial_summary: NOV Inc. is a mid-cap energy business with a $6.3B market cap on $8.7B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +7% over the past three years and -5% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.

Returns on capital run at 4% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, and 21% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $876M in free cash flow — roughly 10 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 8.63× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -9.8% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.2× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 5.6×.

Management returns a meaningful 8.1% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 6% operating margin trails the Energy median (16%) by 10pp, so it is a below-average operator in its field.
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.52x).
It accounts for 0.2% of sector revenue and 0.1% of sector operating profit.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.05 across 202 companies in the universe; the top four hold 40% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 26% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 12% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 20% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 36% and a beta of 0.89, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.12 vs 5y 0.82), so read it loosely.
About $63.9M trades a day, enough to build a position.

val: The stock trades 35% below its DCF fair value of $26.83, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 6%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $20.46 to $36.00 (P10-P90).
Multiples send mixed signals against Energy peers: cheaper on P/FCF 7.1 vs 14.3, richer on P/E 42.8 vs 13.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 13% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 14.0% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 6.6% (vs the 8% bar).
The 20 covering analysts target $22.25 on average, 27% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 4% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.0%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 62.48).
It runs a 21% gross margin and converts 10% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is a concern: high accruals (-9.8% of assets).
ROE of 2% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.8x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 18pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 0.8% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.2x net debt to EBITDA ($1.6B of cash against $1.7B of debt), with interest covered 5.6x.

growth: Revenue has compounded at 6.5% over 3 years, 7.5% over 5 years and -5.1% over 10 years, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 22%).
At current returns, reinvesting 4% of profits supports about 0.2% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 4.6% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.00, a backlog worth 55% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 15%.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.1x, 4.3% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 17, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.7%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only sold over the past year (6 sales, net $4.6M sold).
It returns 8.1% a year to shareholders (5.0% in buybacks and 2.1% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 1.9% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It pays out 106% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
Short interest is elevated at 14.3% of the float, 8.0 days to cover.
people: With about 31,605 employees, each generates about $277K of revenue, 0.1x the Energy median, and productivity has fallen 2.3% a year.

CEO pay is $1.6M (6x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
